content: Stamford Hospital is a private, nonprofit institution located in Stamford, Connecticut. It serves as both a community hospital and a teaching hospital, with affiliations to 440 physicians. The hospital has 305 inpatient beds distributed across various departments, including medicine, surgery, obstetrics/gynecology, psychiatry, and critical care units for both medical and surgical patients. As of 2005, the hospital employed 2,254 individuals. Adjacent to the hospital, the Tandet Center, a nursing home previously operated by Stamford Hospital, was sold in recent years. The Tandet Center's workforce of 65 employees, along with 100 hospital employees, are represented by the New England Health Care Employees Union, District 1199, which is affiliated with the Service Employees International Union. Employees who utilize the hospital's services receive care without a deductible. The hospital is led by its president, Brian Grissler. In early 2007, Stamford Hospital launched the Familial Colorectal Cancer Registry, a private initiative aimed at individuals and families with a history of colorectal or related cancers. This registry, the first of its kind in Connecticut, provides members with general screening information, updates on the latest research, and access to a dedicated website. In 2004, the hospital received the Ernest A. Codman Award from the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations. This recognition was for the development of a protocol to maintain optimal blood glucose levels in critically ill patients, which resulted in a 29% reduction in mortality rates and an 11% decrease in intensive care unit stays. In 2005, the American Nursing Credentialing Center awarded Stamford Hospital for excellence in nursing services, making it one of only 168 hospitals nationwide to receive this honor. In 2007, Ernst & Young LLP recognized Brian Grissler with the Entrepreneur of the Year award in the social enterprise category. The hospital's Cardiology Department, which has 32 beds, expanded its services in August 2005 to include emergency angioplasty. By early 2007, the hospital was prepared to offer open-heart surgery and elective angioplasty. The Richard & Hinda Rosenthal Cardiology Unit, a 24-bed facility, was recently opened to provide care for more acute cardiac patients in a setting designed to feel warmer and more home-like. This unit includes eight specialized beds for patients requiring advanced care. The Daniel P. & Grace I. Tully & Family Health Center, located at 32 Strawberry Hill Avenue, opened in the spring of 2002 on the site of the former St. Joseph's Hospital. This facility, named after the Tully family in recognition of their significant donation, offers a range of services, including diagnostic imaging, ambulatory surgery, the Women's Breast Center, the Heart Institute, the Professional Pharmacy, the Southern Connecticut Vascular Center, the Immediate Care Center, outpatient mental health services, and the Health & Fitness Institute. At 26 Palmer's Hill Road, Stamford Hospital operates the Rehab Center, the Children's Health Center, adult day services, and Skill Source. In June 2006, the hospital opened the Darien Imaging Center at 6 Thorndal Circle to provide outpatient radiology services. Stamford Hospital has several alliances and partnerships. It is a member of the NewYork-Presbyterian Healthcare System and serves as a major teaching affiliate of Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons. The hospital supports teaching programs in internal medicine, family practice, psychiatry, obstetrics/gynecology, and surgery. Additionally, it is part of the Planetree Alliance, a network of hospitals focused on patient-centered care. Stamford Hospital was established on May 7, 1896, with 30 beds in a mansion on East Main Street, west of the railroad bridge. The hospital's founding was made possible by John Clasen, a farmer, former state legislator, town assessor, and school board member, who sold some of his property to raise $45,000 for the institution. Clasen was inspired to create the hospital after consulting with his friend and attorney, Edwin L. Scofield, who later became Stamford's second mayor. Clasen stipulated that the hospital be named Stamford Hospital, remain nonsectarian, and not discriminate against patients. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, Stamford Hospital faced significant financial challenges. Between 1994 and 2000, the hospital experienced financial losses in six out of seven years, including a $22 million deficit in one year. By 2001, the hospital's pension plan was underfunded by $40 million. Brian Grissler assumed the role of president and CEO in 2001. In response to financial difficulties, approximately 200 employees were laid off in 2002 and 2003, and the hospital was losing market share. However, under Grissler's leadership, the hospital's financial situation improved, with revenues reaching $357 million in 2007. That same year, Grissler was honored with Ernst & Young LLP's Entrepreneur of the Year award in the social enterprise category.
